plan.why: High-search brand question with a fresh hook, in our 'X vs Y' title format. The body rests on settled NEJM trials, so it should pass the fact-check. | fact-check: I checked the hook facts. The Medscape headline is 'Oral Semaglutide Obesity Rx Tops 100K Monthly in 2 Months'. That counts monthly NEW prescriptions, reached within 2 months of launch: https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/oral-semaglutide-obesity-rx-tops-100k-monthly-2-months-2026a100124c. The JAMA Netw Open study is 'Early Adoption and Diffusion of Oral Semaglutide in US Adults With Obesity', published Oct 7, 2026: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2854937. It reports that people starting the pill were older, more often female, had a lower BMI and were more often on Medicare. The '>80% new to GLP-1 therapy' figure is Novo Nordisk's own press-release number (3 million prescriptions, ADA 2026). Credit it to the company, not to JAMA. FDA approved the pill on Dec 22, 2025, and it launched in the US in Jan 2026. Limit the approval status to the US unless other countries are re-checked when the script is written. Problem: the title 'Which One Works Better?' promises a verdict that two separate trials can't give, so the content can't pay it off. Use only OASIS 4, the trial of the approved pill. Don't use OASIS 1, which tested a higher oral dose that isn't the approved product. Give each trial its own population, length (64 vs 68 weeks) and placebo figure. Describe SNAC only as the label or papers do: it buffers the stomach locally, protects the drug from enzymes and helps absorption through the stomach lining, and only a small share is absorbed. Give no mg strengths and no fasting or water instructions.

package.description:
Quick answer: In separate trials (not head-to-head), the daily semaglutide pill cut average body weight 13.6% at 64 weeks (OASIS 4) and the weekly shot 14.9% at 68 weeks (STEP 1), vs 2.2-2.4% on placebo. Side effects were mostly gut-related, mostly mild to moderate and temporary, in both trials. We can't crown a winner.

This video is general education, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either form is right for you. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
1. Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults with Overweight or Obesity (STEP 1), NEJM, 2021 - https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2032183
2. Oral Semaglutide at a Dose of 25 mg in Adults with Overweight or Obesity (OASIS 4), NEJM, 2025 - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40934115/
3. Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Obesity without Diabetes (SELECT), NEJM, 2023 - https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307563
4. Early Adoption and Diffusion of Oral Semaglutide in US Adults With Obesity, JAMA Network Open, 2026 - https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2854937

script.working_title: Semaglutide Pill vs Shot (Wegovy): What the Trials Show
script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity: a launch number (100,000+ new prescriptions within 2 months, from Medscape and Johns Hopkins), followed by an open loop. One number lands almost exactly the same for the pill and the shot, and it pays off in the side-effects chapter.

scenes.narration: Within 2 months of its US launch, a weight-loss pill passed 100,000 new prescriptions. It's semaglutide, the very same molecule inside the Wegovy shot. You just swallow it instead of injecting it.
So the question everyone's asking is simple. If it's the same drug, does the pill work as well as the shot?

visual.stock_query: cartoon pill and pen face off

scenes.narration: Over the next few minutes, we'll put the 2 landmark trials side by side. STEP 1 tested the weekly shot. OASIS 4 tested the daily pill.
You'll see the weight loss, the side effects, and the everyday differences that might make one form suit you better than the other.
First, an honest warning. These were separate trials, not a head-to-head race. So we can compare them carefully, but we can't crown a winner.

visual.myth: The pill and the shot were tested head-to-head

scenes.narration: And stay with me, because there's one number where the pill and the shot land almost exactly on top of each other. It's probably not the one you'd guess.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop (paid off in Side effects compared)

scenes.narration: First, what is semaglutide? It's a lab-made version of GLP-1, a hormone your gut releases after you eat.
GLP-1 signals to the appetite centers in your brain. It slows how fast your stomach empties. And it helps your pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises.

visual.stock_query: brain stomach pancreas connected by arrows

scenes.retention_device: Fast list to keep the visuals moving

scenes.narration: But your body's own GLP-1 lasts only minutes before an enzyme called DPP-4 breaks it down.
Semaglutide was engineered to resist that. Its half-life is about 1 week, so the shot is given just once a week, under the skin.

visual.stock_query: calendar week with one pen icon

scenes.narration: But sending that same molecule through your stomach? That's a much harder trick. And this is where it gets clever.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: 'this is where it gets clever'

scenes.narration: Semaglutide is a peptide, basically a small protein. And your stomach is built to break proteins down, using acid and digestive enzymes.
So the pill carries a helper molecule called SNAC. Right around the dissolving tablet, it buffers the stomach locally, which helps shield semaglutide from those enzymes.
SNAC also helps semaglutide cross the stomach lining into the blood. According to the label, most of the absorption happens in the stomach itself.
Even with that help, only a small share of each dose gets absorbed. That's why the pill contains much more semaglutide than a weekly shot, and it's taken once a day.

visual.stock_query: big pill small trickle into bloodstream

scenes.narration: Because absorption is so delicate, the pill comes with its own daily routine for taking it. Your prescriber or pharmacist will walk you through it.
Here's a twist most people miss: the semaglutide pill isn't brand new. A version called Rybelsus has been approved for type 2 diabetes since 2019, used at different doses.

visual.stat_label: Oral semaglutide approved for type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: What's new is the weight-management version. The FDA approved it in the US on Dec 22, 2025, and it launched in January 2026.

visual.stat_label: FDA approval of the semaglutide weight pill

scenes.narration: So that's one molecule with two very different routes into your body. Now for the part that matters most: what happened to people's weight. Let's start with the shot.
STEP 1 was published in 2021 in the New England Journal of Medicine. It enrolled 1,961 adults.
All of them had obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related health condition. None had diabetes.

visual.stock_query: diverse adults in clinic waiting room

scenes.narration: Everyone got lifestyle support: a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. Then 2 out of 3 people were randomly assigned to weekly semaglutide, and the rest to a placebo.
The trial ran for 68 weeks, which is about a year and 4 months.
The result? Average body weight fell 14.9% on semaglutide, compared with 2.4% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Average weight change on the weekly shot

scenes.narration: To picture it: for someone starting at about 220 pounds, a 14.9% drop would be roughly 33 pounds. But that's an average, not a promise.
And 86.4% of people on semaglutide lost at least 5% of their body weight, compared with 31.5% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Lost at least 5% on the shot

scenes.narration: One detail makes these numbers more trustworthy. They count everyone who was randomized, including people who stopped treatment along the way.
Averages also hide a wide range. Some people lost 20% or more, and some lost much less. A trial average can't predict your own response.

visual.stock_query: many different paths down a hill

scenes.narration: So that's the shot. Now for the real test: can a pill that's barely absorbed get anywhere close?

visual.stock_query: small pill at race starting line

scenes.narration: OASIS 4 was published in 2025, also in the New England Journal of Medicine. It tested the daily pill at the dose that became the approved weight-management pill.
It enrolled 307 adults, who again had obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. And again, none had diabetes.

visual.stock_query: smaller group of adults in clinic

scenes.narration: It used the same setup as STEP 1: lifestyle support for everyone, with 2 out of 3 randomly assigned to the pill and the rest to placebo. It ran for 64 weeks.
The result? Average body weight fell 13.6% on the pill, compared with 2.2% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Average weight change on the daily pill

scenes.narration: And 79.2% of people taking the pill lost at least 5% of their weight, compared with 31.1% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Lost at least 5% on the pill

scenes.narration: As in STEP 1, those figures count everyone who was randomized, including people who stopped the pill.
So let's line them up. The shot: 14.9% over 68 weeks. The pill: 13.6% over 64 weeks.
It's tempting to call the shot the winner. But these were different trials, with different people, different sizes and different lengths.

visual.myth: The shot clearly beats the pill

scenes.narration: STEP 1 had more than 6 times as many people, and OASIS 4 was 4 weeks shorter. Differences like these can nudge results either way.
Here's what you can fairly say: in its own trial, each form beat placebo by more than 10 percentage points of body weight.

visual.stat_label: Each form's lead over placebo, own trial

scenes.narration: But weight loss is only half the story. The other half is how people feel while they're taking it, and that's where our mystery number shows up.

visual.stock_query: question mark envelope about to open

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: the main loop is about to pay off

scenes.narration: Since both forms are the same molecule, you'd expect similar side effects. In both trials, the most common ones involved the gut.
In STEP 1, the top ones were nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation. They were mostly mild to moderate, and mostly temporary.
Now for the number I promised you. In STEP 1, 74.2% of people on the weekly shot reported a gastrointestinal side effect.

visual.stat_label: Gut side effects on the shot, STEP 1

scenes.narration: And in OASIS 4, on the daily pill? 74.0%. Nearly identical.

visual.stat_label: Gut side effects on the pill, OASIS 4

scenes.narration: But read the fine print with me. The placebo groups reported gut complaints too: 47.9% in STEP 1, and 42.2% in OASIS 4.
Everyday life brings stomach upsets of its own. That's exactly why trials include a placebo group: to separate the background noise from what the drug itself adds.
In OASIS 4, the gut side effects were also mostly mild to moderate and temporary.

In STEP 1, 7.0% of people on the shot stopped treatment because of side effects, compared with 3.1% on placebo. In OASIS 4, about 7% on the pill stopped because of side effects, compared with about 6% on placebo.
scenes.on_screen_text: Stopped due to side effects: about 7% on each

items: Pill, OASIS 4: about 7% vs about 6% placebo

scenes.narration: So in their own trials, the pill and the shot showed a similar pattern of gut side effects. Once again, these were separate trials, not a head-to-head test.

visual.stock_query: two matching patterns side by side

scenes.narration: If you're on either form, clinical recommendations suggest a few simple habits that can make the early weeks easier.
Eat smaller meals. Stop eating when you feel full. Go easy on greasy, high-fat foods. And keep sipping fluids through the day.
And if side effects are rough or don't settle, tell your prescriber. That's a conversation worth having, not something to push through alone.
So the results look similar, and the side effects look similar. That means the deciding factors may be things no trial table shows.
Difference number 1 is rhythm. The shot is once a week. The pill is once a day, with its own routine.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a numbered countdown

scenes.narration: Some people like a weekly routine and not thinking about it the other 6 days. Others would rather take a daily pill than use a needle, even a small one.
Difference number 2 is who's actually choosing the pill. A study published in JAMA Network Open in October 2026 looked at early adopters in the US.
Compared with people starting the injections, people starting the pill were a little older, more often female, had a slightly lower BMI, and were more often on Medicare.
That describes who reached for it first. It doesn't tell you which form is better for you.

Number 3 is the heart evidence, and here the two forms line up more than you'd think. The SELECT trial tested the weekly shot in 17,604 adults who had heart disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Escalation: a bigger benefit, with a twist

scenes.narration: Over an average of more than 3 years, semaglutide lowered the relative risk of heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death by 20% compared with placebo. In absolute terms, that was 6.5% of people on semaglutide versus 8.0% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Relative risk, major heart events, SELECT

scenes.retention_device: Big surprising stat with its absolute numbers

scenes.narration: That trial used the injection, in that specific group of people. In the US, the Wegovy pill's label also covers lowering heart risk in adults with heart disease and overweight or obesity. If heart protection is part of your reason, ask your prescriber how that applies to you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Both US labels cover heart risk

scenes.narration: And number 4 is the practical side. Coverage, cost and supply vary by plan and change often, so check with your insurer and your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: person on phone with insurance card

scenes.narration: And one thing applies to both forms: these are long-term medicines. Here's what one trial found when treatment ended.
In a STEP 1 extension that followed 327 participants, people who stopped the weekly shot regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost, within a year.

visual.stat_label: Lost weight regained within 1 year of stopping

scenes.narration: That's trial data, not advice. Any change to your treatment is a decision for you and your prescriber to make together.
So which one works better? Here's the honest answer the evidence supports.
Number 1: it's the same molecule. The pill and the shot are both semaglutide, and both act like your natural GLP-1.
Number 2: both had strong results in their own trials. Average weight loss was 14.9% for the shot at 68 weeks and 13.6% for the pill at 64 weeks.
Number 3: the side-effect pattern was similar. It was mostly gut symptoms, mostly mild to moderate and temporary.
Number 4: the real differences are weekly versus daily, a needle versus a pill, and practical things like routine, coverage and supply.
Number 5: get the most from either one. Include protein at your meals, and add muscle-strengthening activity, which US guidelines recommend for adults on at least 2 days a week.
And the most important step: talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either form is right for you, and which one fits your life.
Next up, we'll look at how that tiny pill actually survives your stomach acid, and how to protect your muscle on these medicines. Subscribe to InforMed so you don't miss them.

factcheck.summary:
The script passes, with 4 minor wording and source fixes listed below. I checked the claims that carry the most weight against the sources.

- **Launch figure:** the Johns Hopkins press release (Newswise, Oct 12, 2026) says "surpassing 100,000 new prescriptions within just two months". The study behind it is in Annals of Internal Medicine, not JAMA.
- **Who starts the pill:** the JAMA Network Open study came out on Oct 7, 2026. Pill starters vs injection starters: mean age 53.3 vs 49.7, female 72.7% vs 70.0%, mean BMI 36.6 vs 37.6, Medicare 13.4% vs 9.3%.
- **OASIS 4:** 307 adults, 2:1 randomisation, 64 weeks on treatment. Weight change was −13.6% vs −2.2% on placebo. Gut side effects were 74.0% vs 42.2%, and mostly mild to moderate and temporary. Stopping because of side effects was about 7% vs 6% (ACC and NEJM/PubMed).
- **Approval:** the Wegovy pill approval includes the heart-risk (MACE) indication for adults with established heart disease and overweight or obesity. That supports s61.
- **Checked from my own knowledge of the published papers, not re-fetched today:** the STEP 1 figures (1,961 adults; 14.9% vs 2.4%; 86.4% vs 31.5%; gut side effects 74.2% vs 47.9%; stopping 7.0% vs 3.1%), SELECT (17,604 adults; 20% relative reduction; 6.5% vs 8.0%), the STEP 1 extension (327 people; about two-thirds regained), and Rybelsus's 2019 approval.

**Framing:** the "not head-to-head" caveat is repeated throughout. Relative risk comes with absolute numbers, and SELECT's population is stated correctly. The prescriber line is there, and the stopping data is clearly labelled "trial data, not advice". There is no dosing. The hook pays off with the 74.2% vs 74.0% numbers, and the placebo context is given.

**Source caveats:** the Medscape page is paywalled (HTTP 402), so I could only confirm its title through search. Its headline says "100K Monthly", which is a bit different from the cumulative wording in the press release. The BioSpectrum page gives the approval date as Dec 23 (likely an Asia time zone), not Dec 22.

issues.claim: Within 2 months of its US launch, a weight-loss pill passed 100,000 new prescriptions.
issues.problem: The Newswise/Johns Hopkins press release supports the narration word for word. But the Medscape headline says 'Tops 100K Monthly', which suggests a monthly rate, not a total. I couldn't read the full Medscape article (paywall). The study behind the figure is in Annals of Internal Medicine (Blaha et al., 2026), not JAMA Network Open, so the figure must not be credited to the JAMA study.
issues.fix: Keep the narration as it is: "Within 2 months of its US launch, a weight-loss pill passed 100,000 new prescriptions." Make newswise2026 the first source for s01. If the description credits the number, write "Johns Hopkins analysis, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2026". Never credit it to the JAMA Network Open study.

issues.claim: The FDA approved it in the US on Dec 22, 2025, and it launched in January 2026.
issues.problem: The cited BioSpectrum page dates the approval Dec 23, 2025 (probably the Asia time zone). Other coverage and the JAMA study's start date (Dec 22, 2025) back Dec 22. The listed source gives a different date from the narration.
issues.fix: Keep "Dec 22, 2025" in the narration and on screen. Put jama2026 first in s18's source_ids, ahead of wegovy_pill_approval. If you can, add Novo Nordisk's own US press release dated Dec 22, 2025 as the approval source.

issues.problem: OASIS 4 had 64 weeks of treatment plus follow-up (ACC: 71 weeks in total). Saying 64 weeks is acceptable as the treatment period, but 'ran for' is slightly loose. s38 also says OASIS 4 'was 4 weeks shorter', which compares treatment periods.
issues.fix: s32 narration: "... with 2 out of 3 randomly assigned to the pill and the rest to placebo. Treatment lasted 64 weeks." s38 narration: "STEP 1 had more than 6 times as many people, and OASIS 4's treatment period was 4 weeks shorter. Differences like these can nudge results either way."

issues.claim: Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either form is right for you.
issues.problem: Safety framing is good overall. But a long-form video with a decision framework doesn't say anywhere that these medicines aren't right for everyone (for example during pregnancy, or with certain thyroid cancer histories, which are on the label).
issues.fix: s72 narration: "And the most important step: these medicines aren't right for everyone, for example during pregnancy or with certain medical histories. So talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either form is right for you, and which one fits your life."

audio.soundNotes: Overall music level is already in the target window (-13.5 dB under voice, -14.2 in pauses), so only a neutral multiplier is applied. Most SFX sit correctly at -14 to -18 dB under speech and -6 to -12 dB in pauses; the changes above pull down about 20 cues that measured louder than -14 dB during active narration (several bubbles/swooshes spiked to -5 to -11 dB) and mute 4 redundant, simultaneously-triggered layer cues at two dense transition clusters (246.7 s and 348.6 s) so no more than 3-4 effects stack in one second. Added five bespoke story-beat sounds (opening stat, molecule-route transition, STEP 1 reveal, the SELECT heartbeat, and the subscribe outro) to give key moments a distinct, felt accent without competing with the narrator.

issues: Red X / green check icons pre-judge the comparison (implies shot wins before the video even runs), which risks being misleading since the title poses an open question
Mascot faces are cute but the icons read like a verdict, not a tease
Subhead wraps to 2 lines ("NEW PILL SCRIPTS A / MONTH") but still readable at phone size
Arrow pointing at the pill is a bit generic and doesn't add much emotional pull beyond the number
Red circle highlight near the pill's top is ambiguous — unclear what it's calling out at a glance
Single pill, no visual contrast with a needle/shot, so the 'vs shot' part of the title isn't visually reinforced

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with short, bold, 1-2 line text and a single clear focal character. #0's versus layout is clean but the X-mark/checkmark treatment on pill vs. shot effectively declares a winner (shot) before the viewer watches, which both overstates the actual even-handed 'is the pill as good?' framing of the title and risks feeling misleading if the trial data don't clearly favor the shot — a packaging risk given the brand's accuracy-first rule. #1 (100K) is solid and ties directly to the video's real hook stat, but a bare number with an arrow is less emotionally charged than a direct pain-point question. #2 ('NO NEEDLE?') taps the single strongest, most universal motivator for this audience (needle aversion) with a happy, reassuring mascot, which should pull more clicks from people scrolling who are curious about skipping injections, while being an honest tease (video answers it with real trial/side-effect data) rather than a false promise. Its only flaw — the ambiguous red circle — doesn't hurt legibility of the headline itself, so it's the best balance of CTR and legibility among options that aren't misleading.

issues.claim: The pill and the shot have never been tested against each other in the same trial, only separately
issues.problem: "Never" is an absolute claim that goes beyond the verified script. The script only says these two trials were separate, not head-to-head. Our craft notes also ban absolute wording.
issues.fix: These numbers come from separate trials, not a head-to-head test: 13.6% average weight loss for the pill at 64 weeks (OASIS 4), 14.9% for the shot at 68 weeks (STEP 1). Save this for your next appointment. This is general education, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either form is right for you. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.
